questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations
questions.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda -3 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =1,\,-3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-3)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
questions.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=4,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$

$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-15,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-15)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-(-15)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}12 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

$$

$$

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
